labels.paceNote: Rounded average race paces, not easy-run or interval targets. To finish under a time, your actual average must be faster than the exact boundary. Terrain, weather and the distance you run also matter.
labels.vdotTool: Check training paces from a recent result
labels.stageNote: Add the stages to your calendar separately. Start the 10K stage when its opening week feels manageable; repeat or extend the foundation stage as needed.
labels.freeNote: The full schedule is free to read. Add the official plan to your calendar for free and start training.
labels.screenshotNote: Web and iPhone · product screens with example training data
labels.sourceNote: These are Trainingload.ai schedules. NHS guidance explains the run–walk approach and allowing more than nine weeks; Polar highlights an easy-running base before a 10K block. Neither source endorses this plan.

couch-to-5k-training-plan.title: What comes after Couch to 5K?
couch-to-5k-training-plan.intro: Finishing the programme is a starting point, not a deadline to race farther. Thirty minutes of running is not automatically 5K.

items.title: Make your first 5K feel repeatable
items.text: Keep practising comfortable continuous runs before adding distance or speed. The 5K hub helps you choose between a first finish and an improvement block.

items.title: Build toward 10K in stages
items.text: Use the Couch to 10K route to see the foundation stage, the readiness check and the later 10-week block together.

5k-training-plan.title: After your first 5K: faster, or farther?
5k-training-plan.intro: Choose one next goal so your training has a clear purpose. You do not need to increase distance and intensity together.

items.title: Run a faster 5K
items.text: The 8-week intermediate plan adds controlled intervals and tempo work for runners with a repeatable running base and a recent result.

items.title: Move from 5K to 10K
items.text: Keep three running days and gradually extend the long run. Check the opening workload before moving into the 10-week plan.

5k-training-plan-intermediate.title: Working toward a sub-25 or sub-20 5K?
5k-training-plan-intermediate.intro: A sub-25 5K needs an average faster than 5:00/km; sub-20 needs faster than 4:00/km. Those are race boundaries, not the pace for every session.

items.title: Start with current fitness
items.text: Use a recent race result to estimate training paces. The same eight-week structure is not a promise of either finish time; your starting point and ability to recover matter.

items.title: Make race pacing explicit
items.text: Check kilometre splits separately from easy, tempo and interval work. If the current workload is not repeatable, return to the first-finish plan before adding faster sessions.

10k-training-plan.title: Which 10K training plan fits your starting point?
10k-training-plan.intro: This beginner schedule takes 10 weeks and three runs per week. A shorter calendar or a faster goal needs a different starting base.

items.title: Already comfortable at 5K
items.text: See how the first week, the 45–65 minute long-run progression and recovery days bridge the gap to 10K.

items.title: Starting with walking
items.text: Build continuous running first, then check readiness for the 10K block. The Couch to 10K route combines both stages without a fixed completion deadline.

items.title: Looking for an 8-week intermediate plan
items.text: Use the dedicated improvement block if you already have a consistent running base. It is a separate schedule, not this beginner plan with two weeks removed.

half-marathon-training-plan.title: First half marathon, 12-week build, or sub-2 goal?
half-marathon-training-plan.intro: The 14-week beginner plan focuses on finishing. Choose a different block when you already have the endurance and want to improve your time.

items.title: 12-week intermediate half marathon plan
items.text: For established runners, the improvement block adds more specific work. Compare its opening week with your recent training before choosing it.

items.title: Sub-2 hour half marathon
items.text: A two-hour half marathon averages about 5:41/km. The goal-time page explains this pace, readiness and the 14-week target schedule.

marathon-training-plan.title: Choose your 18-week marathon build
marathon-training-plan.intro: Eighteen weeks describes the length, not the difficulty. A first marathon, a personal best and a specific finish time call for different preparation.

items.title: Improve on a previous marathon
items.text: Use the intermediate block when a consistent running base and longer runs are already in place. Check the actual weekly workload before committing.

items.title: Work toward sub-4 or sub-3
items.text: Four hours averages about 5:41/km; three hours about 4:16/km. A pace calculation alone cannot establish readiness for either goal.

improve-10k.title: An 8-week intermediate 10K plan: is it the right step?
improve-10k.intro: This is an improvement block for an established running routine. Compare week 1 with your recent training, including the quality sessions and the time available for recovery.

items.title: If your first 10K is still the goal
items.text: Choose the 10-week, three-run beginner plan when extending comfortable running is the priority.

items.title: If you have a finish time in mind
items.text: Use the target page to compare sub-40, sub-45 and sub-50 race averages, then assess them against a recent result.

faq: Can I use this 8-week plan as a complete beginner?
No. Eight weeks is the length of this intermediate block, not a shortcut from no running. Start with the foundation or beginner schedule if week 1 is beyond your current routine.
Should I use the example pace printed in the schedule?
The public pace example uses VDOT 40 for illustration. It is not your prescription. Use a recent result to establish training paces and keep easy days conversational.

target-10k.title: Sub-40, sub-45 or sub-50 10K: turn the goal into a pace
target-10k.intro: The 10-week target block is a shared structure, not three separate guaranteed-result plans. Check the required race pace against your recent performance before choosing a goal.

items.title: Use evidence from a recent race
items.text: A recent 5K or 10K helps you judge the gap. Use it to estimate current training paces rather than forcing every run to match the goal average.

items.title: Keep first-finish and time goals separate
items.text: If comfortable continuous running is still developing, use the beginner plan first. You can choose a time-focused block once that workload is repeatable.

faq: What pace do I need for a sub-50 10K?
Faster than 5:00 per kilometre on average. Sub-45 requires faster than 4:30/km, and sub-40 faster than 4:00/km. These are race averages, not easy-run targets.
Does this plan guarantee a sub-40 or sub-50 result?
No. The ten-week schedule cannot guarantee a finish time. Your recent performance, training consistency, recovery and race conditions all affect the outcome.

improve-half-marathon.title: How to use a 12-week intermediate half marathon plan
improve-half-marathon.intro: Start this block with a settled running routine. The twelve weeks are for developing race fitness, not building all of your endurance from scratch.

items.title: Check the opening week
items.text: Look at the long run and the quality sessions together. If they represent a large jump from recent training, allow more foundation time.

items.title: Choose a realistic time goal
items.text: If you are considering sub-2, compare its race pace with a recent result and your longer-run endurance before moving to the target block.
items.link: See the half marathon target plan

faq: Can I shorten the beginner plan to twelve weeks?
This is a separate intermediate schedule. Removing weeks from the fourteen-week beginner plan removes part of its progression; it does not turn it into this plan.
Should my long runs be at half marathon goal pace?
Not by default. Follow the effort and structure of each session. Goal pace is not a substitute for the easy-running prescription.

target-half-marathon.title: A sub-2 hour half marathon starts with a realistic pace
target-half-marathon.intro: Two hours over 21.0975 km averages about 5:41/km or 9:09/mile. This 14-week goal-time block helps organise preparation; the goal still needs to fit your current fitness.

items.title: Check both speed and endurance
items.text: A recent 5K or 10K gives a useful reference, but a prediction does not show whether you can sustain that effort over 21.1 km. Review longer runs and recovery too.

items.title: Choose a first-finish plan when needed
items.text: If the goal-time workload is too large a jump, the beginner plan keeps the focus on building endurance for your first finish.

faq: Is 5:41/km enough for a sub-2 half marathon?
It is a rounded reference. The exact two-hour boundary is about 5:41.27/km; your average must be faster than that, and the distance you actually run may exceed 21.0975 km.
Do I run every session at sub-2 pace?
No. Easy running, longer runs and quality sessions have different purposes. Follow their prescribed effort rather than using race pace everywhere.

improve-marathon.title: An 18-week intermediate marathon plan needs an existing base
improve-marathon.intro: The calendar gives you time to build, practise fueling and taper. It does not replace the running consistency needed to handle week 1.

items.title: Check the whole week, not just the long run
items.text: Compare the opening schedule with recent weeks and leave room for recovery. Extra missed sessions should not be stacked onto the next week.

items.title: Separate improvement from a finish-time promise
items.text: Use the target plan when you have a specific time backed by recent performance. Sub-4 and sub-3 require substantially different race paces.

faq: Is an 18-week marathon plan suitable for beginners?
There is a separate eighteen-week first-finish plan. This intermediate version assumes an established running routine; compare the actual opening workload rather than choosing by duration alone.
Should I add extra long runs to improve faster?
Follow the planned progression and recovery days. Adding another long run increases workload without guaranteeing a better result, especially when you are already struggling to recover.

target-marathon.title: Sub-4 or sub-3 marathon: choose the goal before the pace
target-marathon.intro: Four hours averages about 5:41/km; three hours about 4:16/km. This 18-week goal-time structure must be matched to your current fitness, endurance and recovery.

items.title: Check more than a predicted finish time
items.text: A recent half marathon is useful evidence, but a calculator cannot assess fueling, durability or how you recover from long runs.

items.title: Keep training pace tied to current ability
items.text: Do not use the desired marathon average for every easy run. Training pace guidance should come from recent performance and the purpose of each session.

faq: What pace is a sub-4 or sub-3 marathon?

Over 42.195 km, the exact four-hour boundary is about 5:41.27/km and the three-hour boundary about 4:15.95/km. A sub-time finish requires a faster average; the table rounds these values for readability.
Is the same schedule a guaranteed sub-3 and sub-4 plan?

No. It is a goal-time training structure. The appropriate workload and intensity depend on current ability, and neither finish time is guaranteed. Use the first-finish plan if this block exceeds your base.

5k-to-10k-training-plan.metaDescription: Move from a comfortable 5K to your first 10K with a free 10-week plan: three runs a week, a readiness check, full workouts and calendar access.
heading: 5K to 10K
training plan.
5k-to-10k-training-plan.intro: Already comfortable running 5K? Build toward 10K over ten weeks with three runs a week, recovery days and a gradual long-run progression.
readiness: You can repeat an easy 5K or roughly 30–40 minutes of continuous running; one all-out 5K is not the same base.
The opening week contains two easy runs and a 45-minute long-run session. Check that this is manageable alongside your recent training.
You can leave recovery days between runs. If fatigue is carrying over or pain changes your stride, do not increase the workload.

stages.title: Keep the running rhythm
stages.text: Begin with three separated running days. Keep the shorter sessions easy while you become comfortable with the opening workload.

stages.title: Extend the long run
stages.text: The long-run labels progress from 45 minutes to a 65-minute peak in week 7. Weeks 4, 6 and 8 include controlled steady work, not all-out intervals.

stages.title: Arrive ready for 10K
stages.text: Reduce the load before race week and start the final 10K conservatively. Short walk breaks are allowed; the aim is completing the distance.

faq: How long does it take to go from 5K to 10K?
This block is ten weeks for runners who already have an easy-running base. You may need extra foundation or repeat weeks; a single 5K finish does not establish readiness for a fixed race date.
Can I train for 10K three days a week?
This official schedule uses three running days, usually separated by rest. Most sessions are easy or long; short steady work appears in weeks 4, 6 and 8.
Can I complete the transition in six or eight weeks?
Do not remove recovery or build weeks to fit a date. The separate eight-week 10K improvement plan is for established runners and is not a shortened version of this first-finish progression.
Do I need to run a full 10K before race day?
Not in this plan. The longest training run is labelled 65 minutes and is effort-based; the distance covered depends on your pace. The final session is 10K.
How is this different from the beginner 10K page?
It uses the same official finish-10k workouts. This page explains the transition from an existing 5K base; the 10K hub compares beginner, intermediate and goal-time options.

couch-to-10k-training-plan.metaTitle: Couch to 10K Training Plan | Free Beginner Progression
couch-to-10k-training-plan.metaDescription: Start with walking and running, build continuous running, then progress to 10K. Two free schedules, three runs a week and a clear readiness check.
heading: Couch to 10K.
Start with walking.
couch-to-10k-training-plan.intro: First build a running habit with nine weeks of run–walk training. When continuous running feels comfortable, move into the ten-week 10K plan.
couch-to-10k-training-plan.readinessTitle: The step between the two plans matters
readiness: Finish the run–walk stage with comfortable continuous running. Thirty minutes does not automatically equal 5K; distance depends on pace.
Before starting the 10K block, establish a repeatable easy 5K or roughly 30–40 minutes of running and check the opening 45-minute long-run session.
Allow extra foundation or repeat weeks when needed. Nine plus ten describes the two schedules, not a guaranteed 19-week couch-to-10K result.

stages.title: 01 / Build the habit · 9 weeks
stages.text: Alternate short easy runs and walks, keep three sessions a week and gradually build toward 30 minutes of continuous running.

stages.title: 02 / Consolidate · your own pace
stages.text: Keep the running comfortable and repeatable. Review recovery and the next plan’s opening workload before extending the long run.

stages.title: 03 / Build toward 10K · 10 weeks
stages.text: Use the official first-finish 10K block once ready. It keeps three running days, progresses the long run and includes a taper before the final 10K.

faq: How many weeks does Couch to 10K take?
This route uses a nine-week foundation schedule followed by a ten-week 10K schedule, with extra consolidation or repeat weeks as needed. It is not a fixed nineteen-week promise.
Can I start the ten-week 10K plan without running experience?
No. Its opening week assumes an easy-running base. Begin with the run–walk stage if you are starting from walking.
Is there an NHS Couch to 10K plan here?
No. These are Trainingload.ai schedules. NHS Couch to 5K is a separate programme; the NHS source below explains the run–walk approach, not an endorsement of this 10K progression.
What if I finish Couch to 5K but do not run five kilometres?
That is possible: thirty minutes of running covers different distances at different paces. Consolidate comfortable continuous running before using the 10K readiness check.
Can I add the whole progression to my calendar?
Add the nine-week foundation plan first, then add the ten-week 10K plan when ready. They are two separate official templates, so you choose the transition date.
What if I already run 5K comfortably?
Use the 5K to 10K route and check the opening workload. You do not need to repeat the run–walk foundation just to follow this progression.
